subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Early Earth's conditions let carbon compounds form without life
The cell is the smallest thing that keeps itself alive
Why the first cells are hard to explain
Fatty acids self-assemble into vesicles
RNA was probably the first genetic material
How the dates of first cells and LUCA are estimated
All living organisms are made of cells, so new ones can be predicted to be
Using a light microscope and calculating size
What every cell has, and why
Prokaryotic cell structure
Eukaryotic cell structure
One cell can carry out every function of life
Cells that break the one-nucleus rule
Recognizing cell types and organelles in micrographs
Mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living prokaryotes
Multicellularity evolved many times and brings two advantages
What every virus has in common
The lytic cycle: the host cell does the work, then bursts
The lysogenic cycle: the phage genome hides in the host chromosome
Why some viruses evolve so fast, and what that means for treatment

questions.q: On pre-biotic Earth, ultraviolet light penetrated to the surface far more than it does today. What is the reason for this?
options: There was no free oxygen, so no ozone could form to absorb the radiation.
The methane and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere had destroyed the ozone layer.
Free oxygen was used up oxidizing methane before it could form ozone.
The high temperatures broke down ozone as fast as it was produced.
optionWhy: Ozone (O₃) is made from oxygen (O₂) by ultraviolet light in the upper atmosphere. Pre-biotic Earth lacked free oxygen and therefore lacked ozone, so ultraviolet radiation was not absorbed and reached the surface.

A student who pictures the ozone layer as an independent shield that gases can damage picks this. There was no ozone layer to destroy: ozone is formed from oxygen, and pre-biotic Earth had no free oxygen.

A student who assumes oxygen has always been in the air looks for a reason it failed to make ozone. In fact there was no free oxygen at all on pre-biotic Earth; it accumulated only after photosynthetic organisms evolved.

A student who uses the heat of early Earth to explain every early condition picks this. The higher temperatures were a consequence of greenhouse gases; the lack of ozone was a consequence of the lack of oxygen, not of temperature.
questions.explain: Ozone (O₃) is made from oxygen (O₂) by ultraviolet light in the upper atmosphere. Pre-biotic Earth lacked free oxygen and therefore lacked ozone, so ultraviolet radiation was not absorbed and reached the surface.

questions.q: Which statement gives a reason that viruses are considered to be non-living?
options: They are cells that are too small to hold the organelles needed for metabolism.
They are not whole organisms, and only complete organisms are living.
They carry out no metabolism and can only replicate using a host cell.
They have genes and can evolve, but they do not have a nucleus.
optionWhy: A student who thinks of a virus as a very small cell picks this. A virus is not a cell of any size: it is genetic material in a protein coat with no cytoplasm, ribosomes or membrane-enclosed interior.

A student who regards only whole organisms as living picks this. Being an organism is not the criterion: a bacterium is a single cell and is alive. Viruses are non-living because they lack metabolism and cannot replicate independently, whatever their size or organization.

A virus has no enzymes for metabolism and cannot grow, respond or maintain itself. New virus particles are made by the host cell's machinery, so a virus is not self-sustaining, which is why it is considered non-living.

A student who counts viruses as living because they have genes and evolve looks for a structural reason and picks the missing nucleus, but bacteria also lack a nucleus and are alive. Viruses are non-living because they have no metabolism and cannot replicate without a host cell.
questions.explain: A virus has no enzymes for metabolism and cannot grow, respond or maintain itself. New virus particles are made by the host cell's machinery, so a virus is not self-sustaining, which is why it is considered non-living.

questions.q: Which set of processes is regarded as the necessary requirements for the evolution of the first cells?
options: Catalysis, self-replication of molecules, self-assembly and the emergence of compartmentalization
A single improbable chance event assembling a complete cell with all of its parts at once
Formation of DNA, then transcription and translation, before any membrane had formed
Continuing spontaneous generation of whole cells from non-living matter in pond water
optionWhy: These four processes are the requirements named in the IB guide: reactions had to be speeded up, information-carrying molecules had to be copied, structures had to organize themselves, and a membrane-bound compartment had to separate internal chemistry from the outside.

A student who reads 'spontaneous' as 'all at once' picks this. No scientist proposes a complete cell assembling by chance; the origin of cells is explained as a sequence of processes that could each occur spontaneously.

A student who assumes DNA had to come first picks this. The first genetic material is presumed to have been RNA, and compartmentalization is one of the requirements, not something that came only after a full DNA-based system.

A student who thinks cells still arise from non-living matter picks this. Cells are currently produced only by division of pre-existing cells; the requirements listed in the guide describe how the first cells could have emerged under conditions that no longer exist.
questions.explain: These four processes are the requirements named in the IB guide: reactions had to be speeded up, information-carrying molecules had to be copied, structures had to organize themselves, and a membrane-bound compartment had to separate internal chemistry from the outside.

questions.q: Why was the formation of membrane-bound compartments a necessary step in the origin of cells?
options: It shielded the enclosed molecules from the ultraviolet light that reached the surface.
It allowed the chemistry inside the compartment to become different from that of the outside.
It provided a solid droplet of lipid inside which the first chemical reactions could occur.
It allowed a complete cell to assemble in a single step from the molecules dissolved in the water.
optionWhy: A student who carries over the GCSE idea that a membrane 'protects the cell' picks this. A thin bilayer is no shield against ultraviolet radiation; the importance of the compartment lies in what it does to the chemistry inside.

A membrane keeps self-replicating molecules and their products together at higher concentrations and separates them from the surroundings, so a distinct internal chemistry can develop – the reason the IB guide gives for why a membrane-bound compartment was needed.

A student who imagines fatty acids forming an oil droplet picks this. A vesicle is a hollow sphere of bilayer enclosing water; the reactions occur in the aqueous interior, not in a solid mass of lipid.
A student who thinks the first cell appeared in a single event picks this. Compartmentalization is one of several requirements that combined gradually; enclosing molecules does not make a cell.
questions.explain: A membrane keeps self-replicating molecules and their products together at higher concentrations and separates them from the surroundings, so a distinct internal chemistry can develop – the reason the IB guide gives for why a membrane-bound compartment was needed.

questions.q: Why is RNA, rather than DNA, presumed to have been the first genetic material?
options: RNA formed as single-stranded copies made from the very first DNA molecules to exist.
RNA is simpler than DNA, so it is more stable and survived for longer in the early oceans.
RNA can be replicated and is catalytic, so it could serve as both genes and enzymes.
RNA was needed to code for the proteins that acted as the very first enzymes.
optionWhy: A student who assumes DNA is the original genetic molecule and RNA its copy picks this. The hypothesis is the reverse: RNA carried information first and DNA took over storage later.
A student who equates simplicity with durability picks this. RNA is less stable than DNA; the case for RNA rests on its ability to be replicated and to catalyse reactions, not on stability.

RNA can be copied by complementary base pairing and some RNA molecules, ribozymes, are catalytic. One type of molecule could therefore have acted as both the genetic material and the enzymes of the earliest cells, avoiding the problem of which came first, genes or enzymes.

A student who believes all enzymes are proteins picks this. The point of the RNA hypothesis is that RNA itself catalysed the first reactions; protein enzymes evolved later, and ribozymes still catalyse peptide bond formation in ribosomes.
questions.explain: RNA can be copied by complementary base pairing and some RNA molecules, ribozymes, are catalytic. One type of molecule could therefore have acted as both the genetic material and the enzymes of the earliest cells, avoiding the problem of which came first, genes or enzymes.

questions.q: Stromatolites and microfossils in rocks from Western Australia are among the oldest evidence of cells. Which approach is used to estimate their age?
options: Carbon-14 dating of the carbon left in the fossilized cells themselves
Sequencing the DNA preserved in the fossils and applying a molecular clock
Identifying the fossils as LUCA and reading its age from the family tree
Radiometric dating of the rock using isotopes with very long half-lives
optionWhy: A student who knows carbon dating as 'the' dating method picks this. Carbon-14 decays away within about 50 000 years, so it is useless for rocks billions of years old.
A student who believes DNA survives in ancient fossils picks this. No DNA remains after billions of years; molecular clocks use the genomes of living organisms, not fossil DNA.
A student who thinks LUCA is a specific fossil organism picks this. No fossil has been identified as LUCA, and a family tree does not supply dates; the age comes from dating the rock.
The rock containing the fossils is dated from the decay of long-lived isotopes such as uranium-238, giving an age of about 3.5 billion years and so a minimum age for life on Earth.
questions.explain: The rock containing the fossils is dated from the decay of long-lived isotopes such as uranium-238, giving an age of about 3.5 billion years and so a minimum age for life on Earth.

questions.q: A biologist collects an organism from a deep-sea vent that has never been examined before. Before looking at it under a microscope, she predicts that it will consist of one or more cells. Which statement best describes this reasoning?
options: It is deductive: a specific prediction is derived from cell theory, and examining the organism then tests it.
It is inductive: the prediction is a generalization drawn from the many organisms already examined.
It is unscientific: cell theory cannot be relied on until every living organism has been examined.
It is unreliable: viruses are living organisms not made of cells, so cell theory has known exceptions.
optionWhy: Cell theory is a general theory; predicting that a particular new organism will consist of cells applies the theory to a specific case. This is deductive reasoning, and examining the organism tests the prediction, which is how a theory continues to be tested.

A student who attaches 'inductive' to anything involving observations picks this. Induction built cell theory from many observations; using the theory to predict one new case runs the other way and is deduction.

A student who treats a theory as a guess until every case is checked picks this. A theory's value lies in generating predictions for cases not yet examined; the prediction is tested when the organism is examined.

A student who counts viruses as living organisms picks this. Viruses are not cells, have no metabolism and cannot reproduce independently, so they are not classified as living organisms and are not exceptions to cell theory.
questions.explain: Cell theory is a general theory; predicting that a particular new organism will consist of cells applies the theory to a specific case. This is deductive reasoning, and examining the organism tests the prediction, which is how a theory continues to be tested.

questions.q: In a photomicrograph taken at a magnification of ×2000, a red blood cell measures 15 mm across. What is the actual width of the cell?
options: 7.5 µm
optionWhy: A student who multiplies the image size by the magnification picks this: 15 mm × 2000. That would make the real cell 30 m wide, larger than the image; actual size is image size divided by magnification.
Actual size = size of image ÷ magnification = 15 mm ÷ 2000 = 0.0075 mm, which is 7.5 µm (1 mm = 1000 µm), the typical diameter of a red blood cell.
A student who converts 0.0075 mm to micrometres using a factor of 100 picks this. 1 mm = 1000 µm, so 0.0075 mm = 7.5 µm; a cell 0.75 µm across would be smaller than most bacteria.
A student who converts 0.0075 mm to micrometres using a factor of 10 picks this. 0.075 µm is 75 nm, about the size of a large virus; 1 mm = 1000 µm, so 0.0075 mm = 7.5 µm.
questions.explain: Actual size = size of image ÷ magnification = 15 mm ÷ 2000 = 0.0075 mm, which is 7.5 µm (1 mm = 1000 µm), the typical diameter of a red blood cell.

questions.q: Every living cell has DNA as genetic material, a cytoplasm composed mainly of water, and a plasma membrane composed of lipids. Which statement gives a correct reason for one of these features?
options: The cytoplasm is mainly water so that it forms a stiff gel that holds every organelle in a fixed position.
The membrane is made of lipids because their hydrophobic tails form a barrier to the water-soluble contents of the cell.
The membrane is made of lipids because lipids form a rigid layer that gives the cell its strength and shape.
DNA is the genetic material because it is protected inside a nucleus in every kind of living cell.
optionWhy: A student who pictures cytoplasm as a solid jelly picks this. Cytoplasm is mainly water because water is the solvent for metabolism; organelles move within it and are positioned by the cytoskeleton.

Phospholipids arrange themselves into a bilayer with their hydrophobic tails inward. The hydrophobic interior blocks the passage of water-soluble substances, so the membrane keeps the aqueous cytoplasm separate from the surroundings and controls exchange.

A student who gives the membrane the role of a wall picks this. The phospholipid bilayer is fluid and flexible; it is a barrier, not a support. Strength and shape come from a cell wall, where present, or the cytoskeleton.

A student who thinks every cell has a nucleus picks this. Prokaryotes keep their DNA in the cytoplasm without a nucleus; DNA is the genetic material because it stores information stably and can be replicated.
questions.explain: Phospholipids arrange themselves into a bilayer with their hydrophobic tails inward. The hydrophobic interior blocks the passage of water-soluble substances, so the membrane keeps the aqueous cytoplasm separate from the surroundings and controls exchange.

questions.q: Which description of the structure of a Bacillus cell is correct?
options: The DNA is enclosed by a nuclear membrane inside a small nucleus within the cytoplasm.
The cell wall outside the plasma membrane is built from long parallel fibres of cellulose.
A loop of naked DNA lies in the cytoplasm, and proteins are made on 70S ribosomes.
The DNA loop is wound around histone proteins to package it within the nucleoid region.
optionWhy: A student who expects every cell to have a nucleus picks this. Prokaryotic DNA lies in the cytoplasm in a nucleoid region that is not enclosed by any membrane.
A student who assumes every cell wall is a cellulose wall picks this. The cell wall of Bacillus is made of peptidoglycan; cellulose walls are found only in plant cells.

A Gram-positive eubacterium such as Bacillus has a cell wall, a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, naked DNA in a loop lying in the nucleoid region of the cytoplasm, and 70S ribosomes on which its proteins are synthesized.
A student who thinks 'naked' refers only to the absence of a membrane picks this. Naked DNA is DNA not associated with histones; the prokaryotic loop has no histones.
questions.explain: A Gram-positive eubacterium such as Bacillus has a cell wall, a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, naked DNA in a loop lying in the nucleoid region of the cytoplasm, and 70S ribosomes on which its proteins are synthesized.

questions.q: Which statement about the structure of a eukaryotic cell is correct?
options: The nucleus is bounded by a double membrane with pores, and its DNA is bound to histone proteins.
The nucleus is enclosed by a single membrane that is continuous with the plasma membrane.
The ribosomes in the cytoplasm are 70S, the same size as those found in bacteria.
The cytoskeleton is a rigid, permanent frame of protein rods holding each organelle in a fixed position.
optionWhy: The eukaryotic nucleus is enclosed by the nuclear envelope, a double membrane perforated by pores, and contains chromosomes consisting of DNA bound to histones.
A student who pictures every organelle with one outline picks this. The nuclear envelope is a double membrane with pores; it is continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum, not the plasma membrane.
A student who thinks all ribosomes are alike picks this. The ribosomes of the eukaryotic cytoplasm are 80S; 70S ribosomes are found in prokaryotes and inside mitochondria and chloroplasts.
A student led by the word 'skeleton' picks this. Microtubules and microfilaments are dynamic, assembling and disassembling to move organelles, change cell shape and form the spindle.
questions.explain: The eukaryotic nucleus is enclosed by the nuclear envelope, a double membrane perforated by pores, and contains chromosomes consisting of DNA bound to histones.

questions.q: Paramecium is a unicellular organism that lives in fresh water. Which statement correctly identifies one of its functions of life?
options: Growth: dividing by binary fission, so that the single cell becomes two separate cells.
Excretion: a process not carried out, because removing metabolic waste requires organs such as kidneys.
Homeostasis: expelling water that enters by osmosis, keeping the water content of the cytoplasm within limits.
Metabolism: releasing energy from food by respiration, without building up any new molecules.
optionWhy: A student who sees division as the organism getting bigger picks this. In a unicellular organism the cell is the organism, so division produces two organisms: that is reproduction. Growth is the increase in cell size between divisions.

A student who ties excretion to organs picks this. A single cell must carry out every function of life; the waste products of its metabolism, such as carbon dioxide, leave by diffusion across the plasma membrane.

Water enters continuously by osmosis; the contractile vacuole collects it and expels it, keeping the internal water content within limits. The water is not a product of metabolism, so this is homeostasis rather than excretion.

A student who uses the everyday meaning of metabolism picks this. Metabolism is all the enzyme-catalysed reactions of the cell, including the synthesis of proteins and other molecules as well as respiration.
questions.explain: Water enters continuously by osmosis; the contractile vacuole collects it and expels it, keeping the internal water content within limits. The water is not a product of metabolism, so this is homeostasis rather than excretion.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the number of nuclei in an atypical eukaryotic cell?
options: A mature red blood cell keeps a single nucleus so that it can control the making of haemoglobin.
An aseptate fungal hypha contains many nuclei within one continuous cytoplasm.
A skeletal muscle fibre has a single, very large nucleus to control its whole length.
A phloem sieve tube element is a dead cell, so it has no nucleus and no cytoplasm.
optionWhy: A student who assumes a protein-filled cell must be making protein picks this. The haemoglobin was made before the nucleus was lost; a mature mammalian red blood cell has no nucleus.
Aseptate hyphae have no cross-walls, so repeated nuclear division without division of the cytoplasm leaves many nuclei sharing a single continuous cytoplasm inside one plasma membrane.
A student who holds to one nucleus per cell picks this. A skeletal muscle fibre forms by the fusion of many cells and so contains many nuclei spread along its length.

A student who models phloem on xylem picks this. A sieve tube element is alive, with cytoplasm and a plasma membrane; it is atypical because it has lost its nucleus at maturity, and is supported by a companion cell.
questions.explain: Aseptate hyphae have no cross-walls, so repeated nuclear division without division of the cytoplasm leaves many nuclei sharing a single continuous cytoplasm inside one plasma membrane.

questions.q: An electron micrograph shows a cell about 3 µm long. It has a cell wall, a paler fibrous region of DNA not enclosed by any membrane, many small dense granules, and no membrane-bound organelles. How should the cell be classified?
options: As a plant cell, because a cell wall is found only around the cells of plants.
As a eukaryote, because the region containing DNA must be a nucleus, as every cell has one.
As a prokaryote, because its DNA lies in a nucleoid region and it has no membrane-bound organelles.
As a eukaryote, because prokaryotic cells are too simple to contain any ribosomes.
optionWhy: A student who takes a cell wall to mean 'plant' picks this. Prokaryotes and fungi also have cell walls; a plant cell would show a nucleus, a sap vacuole and other membrane-bound organelles.

A student who believes every cell has a nucleus reads the nucleoid as a nucleus. A nucleus is bounded by a double membrane; DNA lying in the cytoplasm with no membrane is a nucleoid, a prokaryotic feature.

A nucleoid region of DNA without a membrane, the absence of membrane-bound organelles and the small size identify a prokaryote; the granules are 70S ribosomes and the cell wall is consistent with a bacterium.
A student who counts ribosomes as eukaryotic organelles picks this. All cells have ribosomes; the small dense granules are the 70S ribosomes of a prokaryote.
questions.explain: A nucleoid region of DNA without a membrane, the absence of membrane-bound organelles and the small size identify a prokaryote; the granules are 70S ribosomes and the cell wall is consistent with a bacterium.

questions.q: If mitochondria originated as free-living prokaryotes taken into a larger cell, which features would the theory of endosymbiosis predict mitochondria to have?
options: Ribosomes identical to those of the cytoplasm, because the host cell now makes them all.
Naked circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, with the ability to divide independently of the host cell.
DNA wound around histone proteins, because all DNA in the cell is packaged in that way.
A double membrane in which both layers are derived from the vesicle membrane of the host cell.
optionWhy: A student who thinks all ribosomes are the same picks this. Mitochondrial ribosomes are 70S, like those of prokaryotes, not the 80S ribosomes of the eukaryotic cytoplasm, which is a key piece of evidence.

A former prokaryote should retain prokaryotic features: naked circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and replication by dividing in two. Mitochondria show all three, which is the evidence the guide specifies for endosymbiosis.
A student who believes histones are universal picks this. Prokaryotic DNA is naked, and so is mitochondrial DNA; if mitochondria had histone-bound DNA it would count against a prokaryotic origin.
A student who forgets the engulfed cell had its own membrane picks this. The inner membrane is the former prokaryote's plasma membrane; only the outer membrane came from the host vesicle.
questions.explain: A former prokaryote should retain prokaryotic features: naked circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and replication by dividing in two. Mitochondria show all three, which is the evidence the guide specifies for endosymbiosis.

questions.q: Which statement about the evolution of multicellularity is correct?
options: Multicellularity evolved independently in several eukaryotic lineages, including plants, animals and fungi.
Multicellularity evolved only once, so all multicellular organisms descend from a single multicellular ancestor.
Unicellular eukaryotes are transitional forms that will become multicellular given enough time.
Larger body size could be reached equally well by one cell growing larger, so specialization is the only real advantage.
optionWhy: Multicellularity has evolved repeatedly: the closest relatives of plants, of animals and of fungi are unicellular, and several unrelated groups of algae are also multicellular. All plants and animals, and many fungi and eukaryotic algae, are multicellular.

A student who models multicellularity on features that arose once, such as mitochondria, picks this. Plants, animals, fungi and several algal groups each became multicellular separately from unicellular ancestors.
A student who pictures evolution as a ladder of progress picks this. Evolution has no goal; unicellular eukaryotes are abundant and successful, and most eukaryotic lineages have remained unicellular.

A student who imagines a body scaled up as a single cell picks this. A cell's surface area to volume ratio falls as it grows, limiting its size; multicellularity allows a large body made of small cells, as well as specialization.
questions.explain: Multicellularity has evolved repeatedly: the closest relatives of plants, of animals and of fungi are unicellular, and several unrelated groups of algae are also multicellular. All plants and animals, and many fungi and eukaryotic algae, are multicellular.

questions.q: Which feature is shared by all viruses?
options: A capsid of protein enclosing either DNA or RNA, but not both
A cytoplasm in which the virus carries out metabolism
A membrane of phospholipid forming the outermost layer
A genome of DNA together with RNA, as in any living cell
optionWhy: The few features common to all viruses are a small, fixed size; nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA, as genetic material; a capsid made of protein; no cytoplasm; and few or no enzymes. No virus contains both DNA and RNA as its genetic material.
A student who thinks of a virus as a very small cell picks this. Viruses have no cytoplasm and no metabolism of their own; every life function is carried out for them by the host cell.

A student who pictures the capsid as a kind of cell membrane picks this. The capsid is protein. Only enveloped viruses have a lipid layer, and it is host membrane outside the capsid, not a feature of all viruses.

A student who assumes genetic material must be DNA with RNA as a working copy picks this. A virus has one type of nucleic acid, DNA or RNA, never both; many viruses have RNA as their only nucleic acid.
questions.explain: The few features common to all viruses are a small, fixed size; nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA, as genetic material; a capsid made of protein; no cytoplasm; and few or no enzymes. No virus contains both DNA and RNA as its genetic material.

questions.q: In the lytic cycle of bacteriophage lambda, what happens after the phage has attached to a receptor on the surface of an E. coli cell?
options: The whole phage is taken into the cell and the capsid is broken down in the cytoplasm.
The phage DNA passes through the tail into the cell, and the capsid remains outside it.
The phage membrane fuses with the bacterial membrane, releasing the DNA inside.
The phage releases its ribosomes and enzymes into the cell to begin making phage proteins.
optionWhy: A student who applies the entry of animal viruses to phages picks this. A phage cannot cross the bacterial cell wall; the capsid stays on the outside and only the DNA enters.

After attachment, lambda injects its DNA through the tail into the cytoplasm. The head and tail remain outside the cell wall. Only the DNA is needed inside, because the host cell provides everything else for synthesis of new phages.
A student who thinks the outer coat of a phage is a membrane picks this. Lambda has no lipid membrane: its outer layer is a protein capsid, and it delivers its DNA by injection through the tail.

A student who thinks the virus brings its own synthetic machinery picks this. Lambda has no ribosomes; phage proteins are made by the host's ribosomes after host RNA polymerase transcribes the phage DNA.
questions.explain: After attachment, lambda injects its DNA through the tail into the cytoplasm. The head and tail remain outside the cell wall. Only the DNA is needed inside, because the host cell provides everything else for synthesis of new phages.

questions.q: What happens to the DNA of bacteriophage lambda in the lysogenic cycle?
options: It is integrated into the host chromosome and is copied along with it.
It stays as a separate circle in the cytoplasm, like a plasmid, replicating on its own.
It is transcribed slowly, making a few phages that leave the cell without lysis.
It is permanently inactivated, so the cell and its descendants can no longer make phages.
optionWhy: In lysogeny the lambda DNA is integrated into the E. coli chromosome as a prophage. It is replicated with the chromosome at each cell division and inherited by both daughter cells, while the genes for the lytic cycle are kept switched off.

A student who files any extra circle of DNA in a bacterium as a plasmid picks this. The lambda prophage is integrated into the chromosome by integrase and is copied only when the chromosome is copied.

A student who imagines lysogeny as a slow lytic cycle picks this. No phages are produced during lysogeny: a repressor keeps the lytic genes off, and phages are only made after induction, when the cell lyses.

A student who thinks a prophage is a dead end picks this. The prophage remains intact and can be induced, for example by ultraviolet damage to the host DNA, to leave the chromosome and enter the lytic cycle.
questions.explain: In lysogeny the lambda DNA is integrated into the E. coli chromosome as a prophage. It is replicated with the chromosome at each cell division and inherited by both daughter cells, while the genes for the lytic cycle are kept switched off.

questions.q: Why do influenza viruses and HIV evolve so rapidly?
options: Their genome-copying enzymes lack proofreading, and vast numbers of virions are produced quickly.
Their RNA genomes are chemically unstable, so bases change spontaneously between one infection and the next.
They alter their genes deliberately whenever they are attacked by antibodies or by antiviral drugs.
They divide in two every few minutes, as bacteria do, so mutations accumulate over many divisions.
optionWhy: The RNA-dependent RNA polymerase of influenza and the reverse transcriptase of HIV do not proofread, so the mutation rate is very high. Short generation times and huge populations supply many variants, and immune responses and drugs select among them.

A student who links the short life of RNA with mutation picks this. Mutations are copying errors made during replication by enzymes without proofreading, not spontaneous changes to a genome sitting inside a virion.
A student who reads 'the virus adapts' as intention picks this. Mutations are random and occur regardless of any threat; antibodies and drugs then select the variants that happen to survive.

A student who transfers binary fission to viruses picks this. Viruses do not divide; each infected cell releases many assembled virions, and the mutations arise when the genome is copied by error-prone viral enzymes.
questions.explain: The RNA-dependent RNA polymerase of influenza and the reverse transcriptase of HIV do not proofread, so the mutation rate is very high. Short generation times and huge populations supply many variants, and immune responses and drugs select among them.
